Reviewers compare the name, date fields, document number, issuing jurisdiction, portrait, and expiration information with an authoritative record. They also look for alignment and typography that remain consistent across fields, a surface and finish appropriate to the document type, and signs that a layer has been replaced, altered, or printed separately. A machine-readable area should agree with the visible information, but a successful scan alone is not proof that the credential is genuine.

The surrounding process matters just as much. A remote service may compare the presenter with the portrait, check liveness, inspect device and session signals, and query whether the credential is valid, cancelled, or reported lost. An in-person reviewer may ask why the document is being presented, compare it with the account or appointment, and escalate conflicting signals instead of relying on appearance.
